extracted.intended_audience: employers, HR and legal counsel, Federal contractors, and other stakeholders affected by the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for employers on the FTC final rule prohibiting enforcement of most non-competes and the required notice procedures to inform workers that their non-competes will not be enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on enforcing non-competes for non-senior executives
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule prohibits employers from enforcing existing non-competes with workers other than senior executives after the compliance date; enforcement or attempted enforcement is an unfair method of competition under § 910.2(a)(1)(ii) (except where, under § 910.3, the person has a good-faith basis to believe that the final rule is inapplicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule does not require rescission (legal modification) of existing non-competes but makes enforcement of such non-competes (for non-senior-executives) unlawful beginning on the effective date. Actions taken before the effective date are not unfair methods of competition under the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception preserving senior executive non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule allows existing senior executive non-competes to remain in force; the Commission is allowing such existing senior executive non-competes to remain in force and exempts future enforcement of existing senior-executive non-competes from the prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission concluded firms have alternatives for senior executives but chose to permit existing senior executive non-competes to continue in effect; future transactions may rely on other methods (e.g., fixed-duration contracts) to retain executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: No rescission (no affirmative legal modification) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not require employers to rescind (i.e., legally modify) existing non-competes; the rescission requirement proposed in the NPRM was eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission rejected rescission because it would impose unnecessary burdens and cause confusion about retroactivity, contract unwinding, and severability. Instead, the rule prohibits enforcement and requires notice to workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice required by the effective date (timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide notice to affected workers no later than the effective date (i.e., no later than 120 days after the final rule is published in the Federal Register), rather than 45 days after rescission as proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission found 120 days sufficient and practicable for employers to notify workers, and requires prompt notice to reduce chilling effects on worker mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice must be clear and conspicuous
rubrics_metrics.description: The person who entered into the non-compete must provide clear and conspicuous notice to the worker that the worker's non-compete will not be, and cannot legally be, enforced against the worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission emphasized using short, concrete, lay-friendly language and refined the model language to be shorter and clearer. Notice should reduce workers' fears of being sued and increase likelihood of understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required identification of the person who entered the non-compete
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice must identify the person who entered into the non-compete with the worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification is required so workers know which employer is stating it will not enforce a non-compete; the model language and safe harbor facilitate compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted delivery methods for notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice may be on paper delivered by hand, by mail to the worker's last known personal street address, by email (including the worker's current work email or last known personal email address), or by text message to the worker's mobile telephone number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple delivery options ease compliance. The rule also allows use of the worker's last known contact information and permits digital notice. While some commenters opposed text as primary, the Commission allows text as one option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor model language
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule provides safe harbor model language that satisfies the notice requirement; the model language in the final rule uses the phrase '[EMPLOYER NAME] will not enforce any non-compete clause against you.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of the model language provides a safe harbor. Because the model wording does not identify the recipient as having a non-compete, employers can use mass communications (e.g., mass email) instead of determining which employees actually have non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass communication permitted using model wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the model language does not identify recipients as having a non-compete, an employer can send a mass communication such as a mass email to current and former workers to satisfy the notice requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simplifies compliance by avoiding the need to determine exactly who has non-compete clauses; the Commission expressly notes employers can copy-and-paste the safe harbor model notice and send broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption when employer lacks contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers are exempt from the notice requirement where the employer has no record of a street address, email address, or mobile telephone number for the worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule categorically exempts an employer who has no such contact information from the notice requirement to reduce burdens and avoid futile attempts to notify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice to former workers when contact info is 'readily available'
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule required notice to former workers when the employer has the former worker's contact information readily available; commenters found 'readily available' confusing or burdensome, and the final rule retains a practical approach (allows use of last known contact information and exempts employers without contact info).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission accepts use of last known home address, email, or cell phone; it declined to impose wide-reaching burdens (e.g., contacting all former workers regardless of data availability) but expects reasonable efforts when contact info exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility for non-English speakers
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule includes an option for employers to make the notice more accessible to workers who speak a language other than English and responds to commenters requesting clear, concise language in languages other than English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters suggested thresholds (e.g., apply to medium/large businesses with a share of workers who primarily speak another language); the Commission revised the rule to facilitate compliance and accessibility but did not adopt a rigid threshold in the text excerpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of 'individualized communication' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to comments that the NPRM's 'individualized communication' requirement was unclear or burdensome, the Commission removed that language from the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing this term simplifies compliance and avoids confusion about whether individualized, person-specific contact was mandatory in all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: §910.3(b) preservation of pre-effective-date causes of action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission adopts § 910.3(b), which provides an exception for causes of action that accrued before the effective date, clarifying the final rule does not render any existing non-competes unenforceable or invalid from the date of their origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means actions taken before the effective date (e.g., enforcing existing non-competes or making representations related to existing non-competes) are not deemed unfair methods of competition under the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: De facto non-competes and scope clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission removed the rescission requirement partly due to comments about proposed § 910.1(b)(2), which addressed de facto non-competes and raised ambiguity; the Commission revised the language concerning de facto non-competes to clarify the scope of the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule clarifies which contractual terms would be covered as de facto non-competes and avoids imposing a broad rescission duty; employers retain clearer guidance on what constitutes a de facto non-compete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to non-competes considered adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds employers have alternatives for protecting investments and relationships—examples include fixed-duration contracts (for goodwill), NDAs (for client lists), trade secret law, patents, invention assignment agreements, and competing on the merits (pay/benefits/working conditions) to retain workers or clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission repeatedly states these alternatives 'reasonably protect the applicable interest while burdening competition to a lesser degree' because they do not restrict post-employment ability to seek work or start a business. The rule does not limit employers from using trade secret law and NDAs in tandem with other alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission's balancing: benefits do not justify harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on evidence and comments, the Commission finds that the claimed business justifications for non-competes do not justify the harms they cause for either senior executives or other workers—because increased enforceability of non-competes has net negative impacts across measures (e.g., suppresses wages, reduces innovation, increases prices/concentration in some sectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission cites empirical estimates (e.g., rule will increase workers' total earnings by an estimated $400–488 billion over ten years; reduction in physician spending; increase in patents; increase in new firm formation by 2.7%) and emphasizes pecuniary benefits to employers are not a sufficient justification under Section 5. This balancing underpins the regulatory choice to prohibit enforcement and require notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employers' compliance burden minimized by simplified notice design
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule's design choices—model safe harbor language, multiple delivery options, use of last known contact info, exemption when no contact info, removal of rescission and 'individualized communication' mandates, and notice by effective date—are intended to make compliance as easy as possible for employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission explicitly states these features reduce burdens on employers, make the notice requirement practicable even for small businesses, and enable the rule's benefits to begin sooner to mitigate ongoing harms of non-competes.
